meta.ogDescription: The full line is "You dumb hitters. By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it." Attributed to Ted Williams; no primary source found.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder, Hall of Fame 1966
answer.sourceLine: Baseball people have passed this around as a Ted Williams line since at least the early 1980s — but always in a longer form that opens with a jab: “You dumb hitters.” The earliest printing located here is Thomas Boswell’s How Life Imitates the World Series ↗ (Doubleday, 1982), where it is relayed secondhand — “Like old Teddy Williams says…” — and no interview, column or book by Williams containing the sentence has been found.

source.excerpt: … what I was doing until I was thirty years old. Like old Teddy Williams says, ‘You dumb hitters. By the time you know what to do, you’re too old to do it.’
trail: The trimmed one-liner is on every quote aggregator, and Simple English Wikiquote ↗ carries it too — referenced only to Baseball Almanac.
Baseball Almanac ↗ in turn cites Rod Cross’s Physics of Baseball & Softball (Springer, 2011), p. 85, so that trail stops at a modern textbook rather than at Williams.
Searching the full text of Internet Archive’s scanned books separates the two forms. The long version — ‘You dumb hitters…’ ↗ — is the only form printed in the 1980s.

The earliest of those located here is Thomas Boswell’s How Life Imitates the World Series ↗ (Doubleday, 1982), a collection of essays rather than of quotations; Bob Chieger’s Voices of Baseball ↗ (New American Library, 1984) is a quotation compilation, and prints the same full wording tagged “Ted Williams, former outfielder, 1976.”

The trimmed one-liner does reach print, but two decades later: searching the sentence itself ↗ returns it without the jab in Ron White’s 22 Success Lessons from Baseball (2004), John Marlowe’s It Ain’t Over ’Til It’s Over (Arcturus, 2010), Neil Shalin’s Red Sox Triviology (Triumph, 2011) and Bruce Spitzer’s novel Extra Innings (2012).
source.excerptNote: As the passage reads in Thomas Boswell’s How Life Imitates the World Series (Doubleday, 1982): the line sits inside somebody else’s first-person remark, and Boswell is relaying a known saying rather than transcribing Williams. Text as returned by Internet Archive full-text search ↗; the scanned page was not opened directly, and the speaker is not identified in the retrieved text.

source.rightsNote: This is a 20th-century American remark whose earliest located printings are Boswell’s How Life Imitates the World Series (Doubleday, 1982) and Chieger’s Voices of Baseball (New American Library, 1984) — both far too recent for the public domain, and the 1976 occasion Chieger assigns to it has not been identified. Nothing here can be treated as free to reuse on a public-domain theory; short quotation with attribution is the safe course.

author.name: Ted Williams
author.kicker: The hitter who thought hitting was a science
author.heading: Who was Ted Williams?
author.metaLine: 1918–2002 · Boston Red Sox left fielder · Hall of Fame 1966
author.bio: Ted Williams — “Teddy Ballgame,” “the Splendid Splinter” — played left field for the Boston Red Sox from 1939 to 1942 and again from 1946 to 1960, with his career interrupted by military service, and retired with a .344 batting average. He remains the last man to hit .400 in a season, which he did in 1941; he was elected to the Hall of Fame in 1966 and later managed the Washington Senators and Texas Rangers from 1969 to 1972. He treated hitting as a subject to be studied — The Science of Hitting is still the standard text — which is exactly why a needle aimed at hitters who never bothered to learn sounds like him.

No primary source written or recorded by Williams has been located.

misattribution.heading: Nobody stole this one — they just cut it
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a famous name having a stranger’s line pinned to it. It is a case of a line being trimmed until it means something else, and of a sourcing trail that circles back on itself.

items.why: Every printing located from the 1980s begins “You dumb hitters.” The jab is what tells you Williams was talking about batting practice rather than about life. Searching the sentence itself ↗ shows the trimmed one-liner reaching print only from the 2000s on — Ron White’s 22 Success Lessons from Baseball (2004), John Marlowe’s It Ain’t Over ’Til It’s Over (Arcturus, 2010), Neil Shalin’s Red Sox Triviology (Triumph, 2011) and Bruce Spitzer’s novel Extra Innings (2012).

items.who: Baseball Almanac and the sites that copy it
items.why: Baseball Almanac ↗ carries the short version and names as its source Rod Cross’s Physics of Baseball & Softball (Springer, 2011), p. 85 — a modern textbook, not anything Williams published or said on the record.

The sourced English Wikiquote page ↗, where each Williams entry carries a newspaper or book citation, does not list this line at all. Only the looser Simple English version ↗ does, referenced to Baseball Almanac.

The punchline was already circulating outside baseball: Francis Leo Golden’s joke collection Jest What the Doctor Ordered (Pocket Books, 1952) ↗ contains “… know what to do . . . you’re too old to do it.” That does not disprove Williams’s version — it does mean he did not invent the shape of the joke.

misattribution.truthLine: The name is very likely right and the sentiment is unmistakably his — but the sentence people quote has been shortened, and nothing closer to Williams than a sportswriter’s 1982 book ↗ has been found.

context.heading: A jab at hitters, sanded down into a proverb
lead: In Williams’s mouth this was not a wistful thought about growing old. It was shop talk, and it came with an insult attached. The full wording that shows up in every printing from the 1980s is “You dumb hitters. By the time you know what to do, you’re too old to do it” — the complaint of a man who believed hitting a baseball was the hardest single act in sport, that it could be broken down and taught, and that most professionals never troubled to study it until their reflexes had already started to go.

Strip the first four words and the sentence changes species. What is left reads as a general lament that wisdom arrives too late to be spent, which is why it now appears on motivational quote sites beside lines about seizing the day — and why nobody quoting it there mentions batting practice. The trimmed version is the one the internet knows, and the dates line up with that: the full wording is the only form in print through the 1980s, and the short one does not reach a book until the 2000s.
context.detailsSummary: How the sourcing trail actually runs
detailsBody: The chain most quote sites are standing on is short and points the wrong way. Baseball Almanac ↗ carries the trimmed one-liner and gives as its source Rod Cross’s Physics of Baseball & Softball (Springer, 2011), p. 85 — a modern textbook. Simple English Wikiquote ↗ then cites Baseball Almanac. Nothing in that chain is closer to Williams than a secondary work published nine years after his death.

Running the phrase through the full text of Internet Archive’s scanned books tells a different and more useful story, and it is a story about dates. Every printing from the 1980s carries the longer form: Boswell’s essay collection in 1982, Bob Chieger’s Voices of Baseball in 1984, then compilations by David Plaut and Wayne Stewart. The trimmed one-liner turns up in books too, but only from the 2000s — Ron White’s 22 Success Lessons from Baseball (2004), John Marlowe’s It Ain’t Over ’Til It’s Over (2010), Neil Shalin’s Red Sox Triviology (2011) and Bruce Spitzer’s novel Extra Innings (2012). Chieger tags the remark “Ted Williams, former outfielder, 1976,” which is the closest thing to a date anyone offers.

Worth noting without over-reading it: the punchline was already a joke-book gag well before Williams is supposed to have said it. Francis Leo Golden’s Jest What the Doctor Ordered (Pocket Books, 1952) contains “… know what to do . . . you’re too old to do it” in a setting that has nothing to do with baseball. That does not show Williams borrowed it — it shows he was working a shape of joke that was already in the air.
context.pull: Drop four words and a needle becomes a proverb.

sourcesVerified.claim: Simple English Wikiquote lists "By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it." among Ted Williams quotes, with the reference given as Baseball Almanac.

English Wikiquote's Ted Williams page, whose entries carry newspaper and book citations, does not include the line "By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it", and has no Disputed or Misattributed section.
Baseball Almanac lists "By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it." and gives its source as Rod Cross, Physics of Baseball & Softball (Springer, 2011), page 85.

Internet Archive full-text search for "dumb hitters" returns the longer wording "You dumb hitters. By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it" in Thomas Boswell's How Life Imitates the World Series, Bob Chieger's Voices of Baseball, David Plaut's Speaking of Baseball, and Wayne Stewart's Little Red Book of Baseball Wisdom and Gigantic Book of Baseball Quotations; Boswell's text reads "... what I was doing until I was thirty years old. Like old Teddy Williams says, 'You dumb hitters. By the time you know what to do, you're too old to do it.'"
Bob Chieger's Voices of Baseball prints the line and tags it "Ted Williams, former outfielder, 1976".
Thomas Boswell's How Life Imitates the World Series: An Inquiry into the Game was published by Doubleday, Garden City, N.Y., in 1982.
Bob Chieger's Voices of Baseball: Quotations on the Summer Game was published by New American Library, New York, in 1984 (Signet paperback).
Francis Leo Golden's joke collection Jest What the Doctor Ordered was published by Pocket Books, New York, in 1952.
The scanned text of Francis Leo Golden's Jest What the Doctor Ordered contains the punchline "... know what to do . . . you're too old to do it." in a non-baseball setting.

Ted Williams was a left fielder for the Boston Red Sox 1939-1942 and 1946-1960, finished with a .344 career batting average, was the last player to hit .400 in a season (1941), was inducted into the Hall of Fame in 1966, and died on 5 July 2002.

Ted Williams was born 30 August 1918 and died 5 July 2002; his nicknames included "Teddy Ballgame" and "the Splendid Splinter"; he managed the Washington Senators/Texas Rangers franchise from 1969 to 1972.
